items.stem: In forming sodium chloride, what happens to the electrons?
options: One electron is transferred from sodium to chlorine
A pair of electrons is shared
Chlorine gives an electron to sodium
items.answer: One electron is transferred from sodium to chlorine
items.markingKey: A. Na → Na⁺ + e⁻; Cl + e⁻ → Cl⁻.

items.stem: Explain the difference between ionic bonding and covalent bonding.
items.answer: Ionic bonding is the transfer of electrons from metal to non-metal, forming ions that attract; covalent bonding is the sharing of electron pairs between non-metal atoms.
items.markingKey: Ionic bonding is the transfer of electrons from metal to non-metal, forming ions that attract; covalent bonding is the sharing of electron pairs between non-metal atoms. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Distinguish between a cation and an anion.
items.answer: A cation is a positive ion formed by losing electrons (e.g. Na⁺); an anion is a negative ion formed by gaining electrons (e.g. Cl⁻).
items.markingKey: A cation is a positive ion formed by losing electrons (e.g. Na⁺); an anion is a negative ion formed by gaining electrons (e.g. Cl⁻). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Use the charges on the ions (Ca2+ and S2−) to write the formula of calcium sulfide.
items.answer: CaS
items.markingKey: M1 charges balance: 1 × (+2) + 1 × (−2) = 0; A1 CaS.

items.stem:
Sofia measured the electrical current through solutions of sodium chloride of different concentrations using a 6 V supply and graphite electrodes.

Concentration of NaCl / g/dm³ | Current / mA: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
0 | 2 | 2 | 2
5 | 44 | 42 | 41
10 | 81 | 84 | 85
15 | 127 | 125 | 127
20 | 160 | 158 | 162

Calculate the mean current when the concentration of nacl was 5 g/dm³.
items.markingKey: M1 (44 + 42 + 41) ÷ 3; A1 42.3 mA (unit and sensible precision).

items.stem: In an investigation into how the concentration of a salt solution affects how well it conducts electricity, explain why distance between and size of the electrodes must be kept the same in every trial.
items.answer: changes the resistance of the solution
items.markingKey: 1 mark: distance between and size of the electrodes would also affect the dependent variable; 1 mark for the specific reason: changes the resistance of the solution. Then only the independent variable is responsible for any change (validity).

items.stem: Magnesium oxide (MgO) melts at 2852 °C but sodium chloride (NaCl) melts at 801 °C. Both are giant ionic lattices. Use ideas about the charges on the ions to explain the difference, and predict with a reason whether calcium oxide or potassium chloride has the higher melting point.
items.answer: Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ carry double charges, so the electrostatic attraction between ions is much stronger than between Na⁺ and Cl⁻ (single charges) and more energy is needed to separate them. CaO (Ca²⁺, O²⁻) will have the higher melting point than KCl (K⁺, Cl⁻) for the same reason.
items.markingKey: Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ carry double charges, so the electrostatic attraction between ions is much stronger than between Na⁺ and Cl⁻ (single charges) and more energy is needed to separate them. CaO (Ca²⁺, O²⁻) will have the higher melting point than KCl (K⁺, Cl⁻) for the same reason.

items.stem: Write a risk assessment for an investigation into how the concentration of a salt solution affects how well it conducts electricity. Identify two hazards, the risk each poses and how each risk will be reduced, and explain one ethical or environmental consideration.
items.answer: Key hazard(s): low-voltage supply only; small amounts of chlorine may form at the anode – ventilate the room and keep runs short. For each hazard: state what could go wrong, how likely/serious it is, and the precaution. Ethical/environmental: e.g. minimise waste and dispose of chemicals correctly, treat living organisms and volunteers with respect and consent.
items.markingKey: 2 two relevant hazards with the risk explained (e.g. low-voltage supply only; small amounts of chlorine may form at the anode – ventilate the room and keep runs short); 2 a specific precaution for each; 1 relevant ethical or environmental consideration.

items.stem: Define the term "ionic lattice".
items.answer: A regular three-dimensional arrangement of alternating positive and negative ions
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: a regular three-dimensional arrangement of alternating positive and negative ions. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Explain why a dot-and-cross diagram of an ionic compound shows square brackets and charges.
items.answer: Each ion is a separate charged particle; the brackets show the electrons belong to that ion and the charge shows how many electrons were lost or gained.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Each ion is a separate charged particle; the brackets show the electrons belong to that ion and the charge shows how many electrons were lost or gained. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between ionic bonding and covalent bonding.
items.answer: Ionic bonding is the transfer of electrons from metal to non-metal, forming ions that attract; covalent bonding is the sharing of electron pairs between non-metal atoms.
items.markingKey: Ionic bonding is the transfer of electrons from metal to non-metal, forming ions that attract; covalent bonding is the sharing of electron pairs between non-metal atoms. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A student claims that metals gain electrons to form negative ions. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Metals lose outer electrons to form positive ions.
items.markingKey: Metals lose outer electrons to form positive ions. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A student claims that an ionic bond is a bond between one sodium ion and one chloride ion only. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Each ion is attracted to all neighbouring oppositely charged ions in all directions in the lattice.
items.markingKey: Each ion is attracted to all neighbouring oppositely charged ions in all directions in the lattice. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against the view that dot-and-cross diagrams are a useful model of ionic bonding.
items.answer: Useful for showing electron transfer and formula but limited; lattice diagrams are needed for structure.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: show clearly which electrons are transferred and the resulting charges; help predict formulae. Arguments against: electrons from different atoms are identical, so dots and crosses are artificial; do not show the 3D lattice or relative sizes of ions. Supported judgement: Useful for showing electron transfer and formula but limited; lattice diagrams are needed for structure.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A covalent bond in which two pairs of electrons are shared between two atoms, e.g. O=O"?
items.answer: double bond
items.markingKey: A. This is the definition of double bond.

items.stem: A student claims that in a covalent bond one atom gives an electron to the other. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: In a covalent bond electrons are shared; transfer of electrons forms ionic bonds.
items.markingKey: In a covalent bond electrons are shared; transfer of electrons forms ionic bonds. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between a double covalent bond and a single covalent bond.
items.answer: A single bond is one shared pair of electrons (e.g. H–H); a double bond is two shared pairs (e.g. O=O, C=O in CO₂).
items.markingKey: A single bond is one shared pair of electrons (e.g. H–H); a double bond is two shared pairs (e.g. O=O, C=O in CO₂). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem:
Noah used published data to compare the boiling points of the simple molecular hydrides of group 14 (CH₄, SiH₄, GeH₄, SnH₄), measured three times by different laboratories.

Period | Boiling point / K: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3

3 | 175 | 180 | 168
4 | 194 | 207 | 202

State the period at which the repeat readings are least consistent, and calculate the range of the readings at that value. Suggest one way to make the data more reliable.
items.answer: 4 ; range = 13 K; e.g. take more repeats and discard anomalies / use more precise apparatus
items.markingKey: 1 4 ; 1 range = max − min = 207 − 194 = 13 K; 1 valid improvement (more repeats, more precise instrument, control a named variable).

items.stem: State the total number of lone pairs on all the atoms in a molecule of ethene, C₂H₄, and the number of bonding pairs.
items.answer: 0 lone pairs; 6 bonding pairs
items.markingKey: 1 6 bonding pairs (C=C plus four C–H); 1 0 lone pairs.

items.stem: Rafael is investigating how the number of carbon atoms in an alcohol molecule affects the energy released when it burns (using spirit burners heating water). Identify the independent variable in this investigation.
items.answer: number of carbon atoms (methanol 1, ethanol 2, propanol 3, butanol 4, pentanol 5)
items.markingKey: 1 mark: number of carbon atoms (methanol 1, ethanol 2, propanol 3, butanol 4, pentanol 5) (the variable that is deliberately changed). The measured variable scores 0.

items.stem: Carbon dioxide (CO₂) and silicon dioxide (SiO₂) have similar formulae, but CO₂ is a gas at room temperature and SiO₂ melts at about 1700 °C. Explain this difference in terms of structure and bonding.
items.answer: CO₂ is simple molecular: small O=C=O molecules with strong covalent bonds inside but weak intermolecular forces between molecules, so little energy is needed to separate them. SiO₂ is giant covalent: every Si is bonded to 4 O atoms in a 3D network, so melting needs many strong covalent bonds to be broken.
items.markingKey: CO₂ is simple molecular: small O=C=O molecules with strong covalent bonds inside but weak intermolecular forces between molecules, so little energy is needed to separate them. SiO₂ is giant covalent: every Si is bonded to 4 O atoms in a 3D network, so melting needs many strong covalent bonds to be broken.

items.stem: To what extent is it true that ball-and-stick models give a better picture of molecules than dot-and-cross diagrams?
items.answer: Each model shows different features; scientists choose the model that best fits the question.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: show the 3D shape and bond angles; show which atoms are bonded. Arguments against: do not show electrons or lone pairs; sticks suggest bonds are physical rods; atoms are not hard balls; relative sizes are wrong. Supported judgement: Each model shows different features; scientists choose the model that best fits the question. Markbands (8 marks): MYP criterion D (0-8, scaled): 7-8 explains thoroughly how the science is applied to address the issue, discusses and evaluates the implications (moral, ethical, social, economic, political, cultural or environmental), and documents sources consistently; 5-6 explains and discusses; 3-4 outlines; 1-2 states.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "molecule"?
options: The electrostatic attraction between positive metal ions and a “sea” of delocalised electrons
A huge network of atoms all joined by covalent bonds, e.g. diamond, graphite and silicon dioxide
Two or more atoms joined together by covalent bonds
Outer electrons that are not attached to a particular atom and can move freely through the structure
items.answer: Two or more atoms joined together by covalent bonds
items.markingKey: C. "molecule" is two or more atoms joined together by covalent bonds.

items.stem: Lars writes: "When water boils, the covalent bonds between hydrogen and oxygen atoms break." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Boiling overcomes the forces between water molecules; the H₂O molecules stay intact.
items.markingKey: Boiling overcomes the forces between water molecules; the H₂O molecules stay intact. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain why atoms form covalent bonds.
items.answer: By sharing pairs of electrons, each atom gains a full outer shell (stable noble-gas arrangement); the shared pair is attracted to both nuclei, holding the atoms together.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: By sharing pairs of electrons, each atom gains a full outer shell (stable noble-gas arrangement); the shared pair is attracted to both nuclei, holding the atoms together. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: "In a covalent bond one atom gives an electron to the other." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: In a covalent bond electrons are shared; transfer of electrons forms ionic bonds.
items.markingKey: In a covalent bond electrons are shared; transfer of electrons forms ionic bonds. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Ingrid wants to find out how the number of carbon atoms in an alcohol molecule affects the energy released when it burns (using spirit burners heating water). Write a focused research question for this investigation that names both the independent and the dependent variable.
items.answer: How does number of carbon atoms affect temperature rise of 100 cm³ of water per gram of fuel burned?
items.markingKey: 1 mark: names the independent variable (number of carbon atoms (methanol 1, ethanol 2, propanol 3, butanol 4, pentanol 5)); 1 mark: names the measurable dependent variable (temperature rise of 100 cm³ of water per gram of fuel burned – thermometer and mass of burner before/after on a 0.01 g balance) in a question form.

items.stem: Write a risk assessment for an investigation into how the number of carbon atoms in an alcohol molecule affects the energy released when it burns (using spirit burners heating water). Identify two hazards, the risk each poses and how each risk will be reduced, and explain one ethical or environmental consideration.
items.answer: Key hazard(s): alcohols are highly flammable – keep bottles closed and away from flames; wear eye protection; tie hair back. For each hazard: state what could go wrong, how likely/serious it is, and the precaution. Ethical/environmental: e.g. minimise waste and dispose of chemicals correctly, treat living organisms and volunteers with respect and consent.
items.markingKey: 2 two relevant hazards with the risk explained (e.g. alcohols are highly flammable – keep bottles closed and away from flames; wear eye protection; tie hair back); 2 a specific precaution for each; 1 relevant ethical or environmental consideration.

items.stem: Why does graphite conduct electricity?
items.answer: Each carbon has one delocalised electron that can move between layers
items.markingKey: Each carbon has one delocalised electron that can move between layers. Each C forms only three bonds.

items.stem: Explain why graphite is soft and slippery and used in pencils and lubricants.
items.answer: Graphite has layers of carbon atoms in hexagons; the layers are held by weak forces, so they slide over each other easily.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Graphite has layers of carbon atoms in hexagons; the layers are held by weak forces, so they slide over each other easily. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: "Carbon dioxide is a gas because its covalent bonds are weak." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: The C=O bonds are strong; CO₂ is a gas because the forces between molecules are weak.
items.markingKey: The C=O bonds are strong; CO₂ is a gas because the forces between molecules are weak. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Priya wants to find out how to identify the type of structure of four unlabelled white solids (sodium chloride, silicon dioxide, glucose and wax) by testing their properties. Write a focused research question for this investigation that names both the independent and the dependent variable.
items.answer: How does the substance tested affect melting behaviour when heated?
items.markingKey: 1 mark: names the independent variable (the substance tested); 1 mark: names the measurable dependent variable (melting behaviour when heated, solubility in water and electrical conductivity of the solid and of any solution) in a question form.

items.stem: Outline one way in which graphene, isolated by Geim and Novoselov in Manchester (2004) shows how structure determines properties.
items.answer: They peeled single layers of carbon from graphite using sticky tape; graphene is one atom thick, very strong and conducts electricity. A single layer of hexagonally bonded carbon has strong covalent bonds and delocalised electrons, giving strength and conductivity.
items.markingKey: Context (They peeled single layers of carbon from graphite using sticky tape; graphene is one atom thick, very strong and conducts electricity.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: A single layer of hexagonally bonded carbon has strong covalent bonds and delocalised electrons, giving strength and conductivity. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to how structure determines properties.

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against the view that graphene will transform technology within the next ten years.
items.answer: Graphene has great potential but production and safety challenges mean change is likely to be gradual.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: extremely strong, light and conductive; possible uses in batteries, flexible screens and water filters. Arguments against: difficult and expensive to produce large defect-free sheets; other materials are already cheap and established; possible health effects of nanoparticles are not fully known. Supported judgement: Graphene has great potential but production and safety challenges mean change is likely to be gradual.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A lattice of millions of oppositely charged ions held by strong electrostatic forces in all directions, e.g. sodium chloride"?
items.answer: giant ionic structure
items.markingKey: C. This is the definition of giant ionic structure.

items.stem: Explain the difference between graphite and diamond.
items.answer: In diamond each carbon forms four bonds in a 3D network (hard, non-conductor); in graphite each carbon forms three bonds in layers with delocalised electrons (soft, conducts).
items.markingKey: In diamond each carbon forms four bonds in a 3D network (hard, non-conductor); in graphite each carbon forms three bonds in layers with delocalised electrons (soft, conducts). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain why diamond is very hard and has a very high melting point.
items.answer: Each carbon atom is covalently bonded to four others in a rigid giant 3D network; a lot of energy is needed to break the many strong covalent bonds.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Each carbon atom is covalently bonded to four others in a rigid giant 3D network; a lot of energy is needed to break the many strong covalent bonds. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Briefly describe silicon dioxide in sand and glass and explain what it reveals about giant covalent structures.
items.answer: Sand melts only above about 1700 °C, which is why glass-making needs very hot furnaces. Every Si atom is bonded to four O atoms in a giant network, so many strong bonds must be broken to melt it.
items.markingKey: Context (Sand melts only above about 1700 °C, which is why glass-making needs very hot furnaces.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Every Si atom is bonded to four O atoms in a giant network, so many strong bonds must be broken to melt it. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to giant covalent structures.

items.stem: Graphite and diamond are both pure carbon. Use their structures to explain why graphite is used for electrodes and pencil “leads” but diamond is used for cutting tools and drill tips.
items.answer: Graphite: each C bonded to 3 others in hexagonal layers; one delocalised electron per atom conducts electricity (electrodes); weak forces between layers let them slide (pencils). Diamond: each C bonded to 4 others in a rigid 3D giant covalent lattice; many strong bonds make it extremely hard (cutting tools) with a very high melting point.
items.markingKey: Graphite: each C bonded to 3 others in hexagonal layers; one delocalised electron per atom conducts electricity (electrodes); weak forces between layers let them slide (pencils). Diamond: each C bonded to 4 others in a rigid 3D giant covalent lattice; many strong bonds make it extremely hard (cutting tools) with a very high melting point.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "density"?
options: Two or more atoms joined together by covalent bonds
A huge network of atoms all joined by covalent bonds, e.g. diamond, graphite and silicon dioxide
A mixture of a metal with one or more other elements, usually other metals or carbon
Mass per unit volume of a substance, ρ = m ÷ V
items.answer: Mass per unit volume of a substance, ρ = m ÷ V
items.markingKey: D. "density" is mass per unit volume of a substance, ρ = m ÷ V.

items.stem: Briefly explain why alloys are harder than pure metals.
items.answer: Atoms of the added element are a different size, distorting the regular layers so they cannot slide over each other as easily.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Atoms of the added element are a different size, distorting the regular layers so they cannot slide over each other as easily. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: With the help of a specific example, explain why alloys are harder than pure metals.
items.answer: Atoms of the added element are a different size, distorting the regular layers so they cannot slide over each other as easily. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.)
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Atoms of the added element are a different size, distorting the regular layers so they cannot slide over each other as easily. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.) (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Sana measures a rectangular block of lead: 5 cm × 4 cm × 4 cm, with mass 904.0 g. Calculate the density of the block in g/cm³ and in kg/m³.

Priya added different percentages of tin to copper to make bronze samples and measured their hardness with a school hardness tester (depth of indentation).

Tin content / % | Indentation depth / mm: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
0 | 1.37 | 1.39 | 1.33
4 | 1.13 | 1.09 | 1.13
8 | 0.88 | 0.89 | 0.88
12 | 0.67 | 0.67 | 0.63
16 | 0.41 | 0.40 | 0.42

Calculate the mean indentation depth when the tin content was 8 %.
items.markingKey: M1 (0.88 + 0.89 + 0.88) ÷ 3; A1 0.88 mm (unit and sensible precision).

items.stem: Explain, using diagrams of the arrangement of particles, why pure copper is soft and malleable but brass (copper with zinc) is harder, and explain why both conduct electricity.
items.answer: Pure copper: identical ions in regular layers that slide easily over each other when a force is applied – soft and malleable. Brass: larger zinc atoms disrupt the layers so they cannot slide as easily – harder. Both have a sea of delocalised electrons that can move through the structure, so both conduct.
items.markingKey: Pure copper: identical ions in regular layers that slide easily over each other when a force is applied – soft and malleable. Brass: larger zinc atoms disrupt the layers so they cannot slide as easily – harder. Both have a sea of delocalised electrons that can move through the structure, so both conduct.

items.stem: Which alloy is made mainly from iron and carbon?
items.answer: Steel
items.markingKey: D. Steel is iron with up to about 2% carbon.

items.stem: Explain why metals are malleable.
items.answer: The positive ions are arranged in regular layers; the layers can slide over each other when a force is applied while the delocalised electrons keep holding them together.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: The positive ions are arranged in regular layers; the layers can slide over each other when a force is applied while the delocalised electrons keep holding them together. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: With reference to aluminium-lithium alloys in aircraft (e.g. Airbus A350), explain how it illustrates alloys having improved properties.
items.answer: Adding lithium makes aluminium lighter and stiffer, reducing aircraft mass and fuel use. Different-sized Li atoms disrupt the layers (stronger) and lithium’s low density reduces the overall density.
items.markingKey: Context (Adding lithium makes aluminium lighter and stiffer, reducing aircraft mass and fuel use.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Different-sized Li atoms disrupt the layers (stronger) and lithium’s low density reduces the overall density. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to alloys having improved properties.

items.stem: Priya wants to find out how the percentage of zinc in brass affects its hardness. Write a focused research question for this investigation that names both the independent and the dependent variable.
items.answer: How does percentage of zinc in the brass affect hardness?
items.markingKey: 1 mark: names the independent variable (percentage of zinc in the brass (%)); 1 mark: names the measurable dependent variable (hardness – diameter of the dent made by dropping a 500 g steel ball from 1.0 m, measured with vernier callipers) in a question form.

items.stem: "Recycling metals is always better than extracting new metal from ores." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: Recycling is usually better, especially for aluminium and steel, but economics and separation limit it for some metals.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: saves energy (recycling aluminium uses about 95% less energy); conserves finite ores and reduces mining damage; less landfill. Arguments against: collection and sorting cost money and energy; alloys and mixed metals are hard to separate; some metals are used in tiny amounts in electronics, making recovery difficult. Supported judgement: Recycling is usually better, especially for aluminium and steel, but economics and separation limit it for some metals. items.answer: A huge network of atoms all joined by covalent bonds, e.g. diamond, graphite and silicon dioxide

items.stem: Explain why sodium chloride has a high melting point.
items.answer: It is a giant ionic lattice; strong electrostatic attractions between oppositely charged ions act in all directions and need a lot of energy to overcome.

items.stem: Tomás writes: "Graphite conducts electricity because it contains ions." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Graphite has no ions; it conducts because of delocalised electrons between the layers.
items.markingKey: Graphite has no ions; it conducts because of delocalised electrons between the layers. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: "Metals conduct electricity because their ions move through the metal." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: The ions are fixed in place; delocalised electrons move and carry the current.
items.markingKey: The ions are fixed in place; delocalised electrons move and carry the current. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A student says: "Sodium chloride is made of NaCl molecules." Evaluate this statement, using a description of the structure of sodium chloride and an explanation of what its formula means.
items.answer: Incorrect: NaCl is a giant ionic lattice of Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions; each Na⁺ is surrounded by 6 Cl⁻ and vice versa; there are no separate molecules. The formula NaCl shows the simplest ratio of ions (1 : 1), not a molecule. Molecules are found in covalent simple molecular substances.
items.markingKey: Incorrect: NaCl is a giant ionic lattice of Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions; each Na⁺ is surrounded by 6 Cl⁻ and vice versa; there are no separate molecules. The formula NaCl shows the simplest ratio of ions (1 : 1), not a molecule. Molecules are found in covalent simple molecular substances.

items.stem: Draw dot-and-cross diagrams for ammonia (NH₃) and for methane (CH₄). Use them to explain why an ammonia molecule has one lone pair but methane has none, and predict which molecule has the larger bond angle.
items.answer: N has 5 outer electrons: 3 shared with H atoms and 2 as a lone pair. C has 4 outer electrons, all shared with 4 H atoms. Methane has the larger bond angle (109.5°) because the lone pair in ammonia repels the bonding pairs more strongly, squeezing the angle to about 107°.
items.markingKey: N has 5 outer electrons: 3 shared with H atoms and 2 as a lone pair. C has 4 outer electrons, all shared with 4 H atoms. Methane has the larger bond angle (109.5°) because the lone pair in ammonia repels the bonding pairs more strongly, squeezing the angle to about 107°.

items.stem: To what extent is it true that synthetic diamonds grown in laboratories are better than mined diamonds?
items.answer: Lab-grown diamonds are chemically identical and usually more ethical, especially if made with renewable energy, but mining communities’ economies must be considered.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: same structure and properties as natural diamond; avoid mining damage and “conflict diamonds”; cheaper. Arguments against: growing them uses a lot of energy (often from fossil fuels); mining supports jobs in countries such as Botswana; some buyers value natural rarity. Supported judgement: Lab-grown diamonds are chemically identical and usually more ethical, especially if made with renewable energy, but mining communities’ economies must be considered. Markbands (8 marks): MYP criterion D (0-8, scaled): 7-8 explains thoroughly how the science is applied to address the issue, discusses and evaluates the implications (moral, ethical, social, economic, political, cultural or environmental), and documents sources consistently; 5-6 explains and discusses; 3-4 outlines; 1-2 states.

items.stem: Maya plans an investigation into how the percentage of zinc in brass affects its hardness. Describe how the results should be recorded, processed and presented, and explain how the reliability and validity of the conclusion will be judged.
items.answer: Results table with the independent variable (percentage of zinc in the brass (%)) in the first column and repeat readings of the dependent variable with units in headings; calculate means (ignoring anomalies); plot a suitable graph of the mean dependent variable against the independent variable with a line of best fit; describe the trend and compare with the hypothesis; judge reliability from the spread of repeats and validity from how well variables were controlled.
items.markingKey: 1 table with IV, repeats and units; 1 means calculated, anomalies identified and excluded; 1 appropriate graph (line graph/scatter for continuous IV, bar chart for categorical) with line of best fit; 1 trend compared with hypothesis; 1 reliability (spread of repeats) and validity (controls) discussed.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "dot-and-cross diagram"?
options: A different structural form of the same element in the same physical state, e.g. diamond, graphite and graphene
The strong electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions
A positively charged ion, formed when an atom loses electrons (usually a metal)
A diagram showing the outer-shell electrons of the atoms or ions in a substance, with electrons from different atoms shown as dots and crosses
items.answer: A diagram showing the outer-shell electrons of the atoms or ions in a substance, with electrons from different atoms shown as dots and crosses
items.markingKey: D. "dot-and-cross diagram" is a diagram showing the outer-shell electrons of the atoms or ions in a substance, with electrons from different atoms shown as dots and crosses.

items.stem: How many covalent bonds does a carbon atom form in methane, CH₄?
items.markingKey: A. Carbon has 4 outer electrons and shares each with a hydrogen.

items.stem: Which substance has a giant covalent structure?
items.answer: Silicon dioxide
items.markingKey: D. SiO₂ (sand) is a network of Si–O bonds.

items.stem: Explain the difference between ionic bonding and metallic bonding.
items.answer: Metallic bonding is between positive ions and delocalised electrons in a metal; ionic bonding is between positive and negative ions formed by electron transfer.
items.markingKey: Metallic bonding is between positive ions and delocalised electrons in a metal; ionic bonding is between positive and negative ions formed by electron transfer. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Briefly explain why the formula of calcium oxide is CaO but the formula of calcium chloride is CaCl₂.
items.answer: Ca forms Ca²⁺; oxide is O²⁻, so one of each balances; chloride is Cl⁻, so two are needed to balance 2+.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Ca forms Ca²⁺; oxide is O²⁻, so one of each balances; chloride is Cl⁻, so two are needed to balance 2+. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain why hydrogen forms only one covalent bond.
items.answer: Hydrogen has one electron and its only shell holds two, so it needs to share one more electron – one bond.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Hydrogen has one electron and its only shell holds two, so it needs to share one more electron – one bond. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: "Graphite conducts electricity because it contains ions." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Graphite has no ions; it conducts because of delocalised electrons between the layers.
items.markingKey: Graphite has no ions; it conducts because of delocalised electrons between the layers. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain why metals have high melting points.
items.answer: There are strong electrostatic attractions between the positive ions and the delocalised electrons throughout the giant structure, needing a lot of energy to overcome.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: There are strong electrostatic attractions between the positive ions and the delocalised electrons throughout the giant structure, needing a lot of energy to overcome. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain why sodium and chlorine form an ionic compound.
items.answer: Sodium (2,8,1) loses its single outer electron to form Na⁺ (2,8); chlorine (2,8,7) gains that electron to form Cl⁻ (2,8,8); both have full outer shells and the oppositely charged ions attract strongly.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Sodium (2,8,1) loses its single outer electron to form Na⁺ (2,8); chlorine (2,8,7) gains that electron to form Cl⁻ (2,8,8); both have full outer shells and the oppositely charged ions attract strongly. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Kwame writes: "In a covalent bond one atom gives an electron to the other." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: In a covalent bond electrons are shared; transfer of electrons forms ionic bonds.
items.markingKey: In a covalent bond electrons are shared; transfer of electrons forms ionic bonds. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Briefly describe nitinol, a nickel-titanium “shape memory” alloy and explain what it reveals about how alloy structure gives useful properties.
items.answer: Dental braces and stents made of nitinol return to their original shape when warmed to body temperature. The arrangement of the two kinds of atom can change and switch back, a property neither pure metal has.
items.markingKey: Context (Dental braces and stents made of nitinol return to their original shape when warmed to body temperature.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: The arrangement of the two kinds of atom can change and switch back, a property neither pure metal has. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to how alloy structure gives useful properties.

items.stem: Arjun plans to investigate how the concentration of a salt solution affects how well it conducts electricity. State three variables that must be controlled to make this a fair test.
items.answer: Any three of: voltage of the power supply; distance between and size of the electrodes; temperature of the solution; depth the electrodes are dipped
items.markingKey: 1 mark each, max 3: voltage of the power supply – higher voltage gives a larger current; distance between and size of the electrodes – changes the resistance of the solution; temperature of the solution – ions move faster when warmer; depth the electrodes are dipped – changes the area in contact with solution. The independent or dependent variable scores 0.

items.stem: A student claims that when water boils, the covalent bonds between hydrogen and oxygen atoms break. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Boiling overcomes the forces between water molecules; the H₂O molecules stay intact.
items.markingKey: Boiling overcomes the forces between water molecules; the H₂O molecules stay intact. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A sample of iron has a mass of 314.8 g and a volume of 40.0 cm³. Calculate its density in g/cm³.
items.answer: 7.87 g/cm³

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Dot-and-cross diagrams are a useful model of ionic bonding."
items.answer: Useful for showing electron transfer and formula but limited; lattice diagrams are needed for structure.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: show clearly which electrons are transferred and the resulting charges; help predict formulae. Arguments against: electrons from different atoms are identical, so dots and crosses are artificial; do not show the 3D lattice or relative sizes of ions. Supported judgement: Useful for showing electron transfer and formula but limited; lattice diagrams are needed for structure.

items.stem: Evaluate the claim that ball-and-stick models give a better picture of molecules than dot-and-cross diagrams.
items.answer: Each model shows different features; scientists choose the model that best fits the question.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: show the 3D shape and bond angles; show which atoms are bonded. Arguments against: do not show electrons or lone pairs; sticks suggest bonds are physical rods; atoms are not hard balls; relative sizes are wrong. Supported judgement: Each model shows different features; scientists choose the model that best fits the question. items.stem: To what extent is it true that graphene will transform technology within the next ten years?
items.answer: Graphene has great potential but production and safety challenges mean change is likely to be gradual.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: extremely strong, light and conductive; possible uses in batteries, flexible screens and water filters. Arguments against: difficult and expensive to produce large defect-free sheets; other materials are already cheap and established; possible health effects of nanoparticles are not fully known. Supported judgement: Graphene has great potential but production and safety challenges mean change is likely to be gradual. items.stem: "Steel should be replaced by aluminium alloys in car manufacture." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: Aluminium makes sense where mass savings matter (EVs, premium cars) especially with recycled aluminium; steel remains cost-effective for many vehicles.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: aluminium is about one-third the density, reducing mass and fuel use; resists corrosion. Arguments against: more expensive and energy-intensive to extract; harder to repair; steel is strong, cheap and highly recycled. Supported judgement: Aluminium makes sense where mass savings matter (EVs, premium cars) especially with recycled aluminium; steel remains cost-effective for many vehicles.
